search-pathology-applicability.read_scope: Full16page author copy, definitions, models, actual games, limitations and references.
search-pathology-applicability.paper_summary: Nau et al. study how branching, evaluation granularity and nearby-state value similarity jointly affect deeper-search decision errors. Their pathology metric uses true optimal moves, not score changes. Experiments include synthetic trees, controlled endgame heuristics and modified games. Effects depend on setting; isolated deeper-search failures do not establish whole-game pathology.
own_application: Our seven negative q1 contexts are not seven proved minimax pathologies: only fixed-foe trajectory outcomes are known, six cold child intervals remain UNKNOWN.

In five original complete-D2 contexts the q horizon changes the action without a main-depth truncation; in two contexts the original q1 is D1 and a separate larger-time cold D2 changes its action. Keep mechanisms separate.
Absolute static score spread is not paper utility granularity. Rescaling heuristic scores under fixed dynamic terms changes our evaluation, so a numerical precision patch is not a theory-backed cure.

Cannot estimate utility local similarity by substituting correlated static price scores and then claim the paper assumptions hold. Full history/auxiliary keys define states; merging physically identical boards could corrupt both graph and proof.

The existing finite202 census measures exact selected-action errors under a stated dependent distribution. Its q1/capture gain and larger-board fixed-foe trajectory losses can coexist. Neither selects a universal q horizon.

Next decision-changing experiment should separate approximation from budget using fixed nodes/cold roots and stated exposure, not fit a horizon gate to these outcome labels. No new learner/MCTS/metacontroller or complete-WDL admission gate.
search-pathology-applicability.decision: Retain all current candidates/defaults; do not call score oscillation or q1 losses proven pathology. Keep proof goal opt-in.
